excerpt: Not automatically. How fault is actually decided in Georgia and South Carolina red light crashes, and when the other driver shares the blame.
keyTakeaways: Red light runners are not automatically liable for intersection crashes in Georgia or South Carolina. Fault is determined by examining whether the other driver was speeding, made an illegal turn, or failed to exercise caution entering the intersection. Both states apply modified comparative fault rules — Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), South Carolina at 51% or more (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Dashcam and surveillance video, traffic signal timing data, and witness testimony help establish fault; red light camera images exist only at Georgia's twelve permitted intersections and South Carolina has none. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Is a driver who runs a red light automatically at fault for a crash?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Running a red light is strong evidence of negligence, but you must still prove that the violation caused the crash and that you suffered damages as a result. The other driver may also argue that you shared fault — for example, by speeding or driving while distracted.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as your share of fault stays below the threshold. In Georgia, you can recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, you can recover as long as you are less than 51% at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

faqs.question: Is a traffic citation for running a red light admissible in court?
faqs.answer: Not the ticket itself. In both states a traffic citation and any conviction on it are inadmissible in a civil case (Georgia: Howard v. Lay, 259 Ga. App. 391 (2003); South Carolina: S.C. Code § 56-5-6160). What can come in is the other driver's guilty plea to the ticket, which the jury may weigh as an admission — though it is not conclusive and the driver may explain it (Gaddis v. Skelton, 226 Ga. App. 325 (1997); Samuel v. Mouzon, 282 S.C. 616 (Ct. App. 1984)). The responding officer can also testify to what they observed.

faqs.question: What if the other driver claims the light was yellow, not red?
faqs.answer: This is a common dispute. Traffic signal timing data from the city or county traffic engineering department can show the exact signal cycle at the time of the crash. Dashcam footage, red light camera images at the Georgia intersections that have them, surveillance footage from nearby businesses, and witness testimony can also help prove the light was red.

faqs.question: Does South Carolina have red light cameras?
faqs.answer: No. A South Carolina ticket for disregarding a traffic signal must be issued in person during a traffic stop and cannot be based on photographic evidence (S.C. Code § 56-7-35). SCDOT's traffic cameras stream live but are not recorded, so no past footage is available from them; useful video comes from surveillance cameras at nearby businesses, dashcams, and doorbell cameras near the intersection.

faqs.question: What damages can I recover after being hit by a red light runner?
faqs.answer: You may recover economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, property damage), non-economic damages (pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life), and in cases involving extreme recklessness like DUI, punitive damages. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases, with no cap where the defendant intended to cause harm or drove while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)-(g)). South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026), with no cap where the defendant intended harm, pled guilty to or was convicted of a felony arising from the same conduct, or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
